blocks.text: Lesson 6 — Encryption, TLS, data classification and secrets

LEARNING OUTCOME
Protect information in transit and at rest, manage keys responsibly, and prevent secret leakage.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Identify public, internal, confidential and highly restricted data. Collect only what is needed and limit retention and access. Encryption at rest can help protect a lost disk; TLS protects data in transit. Neither replaces correct authorization or makes a compromised application safe.

blocks.text: HTTPS uses TLS to provide confidentiality, integrity and authentication for a network connection. Browsers validate certificate chains and hostnames. Investigate expired, mismatched or untrusted certificates instead of teaching users to click through warnings. Monitor renewals and use current server guidance.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Encryption at rest. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Key lifecycle. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: API tokens, keys, database passwords and recovery codes must stay out of source control, screenshots, client-side code and logs. Use an approved secret store, restrict scope, name an owner, rotate when exposed and revoke unused credentials. If a key leaks, rotate it; deleting a line is not enough.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.question: What does TLS primarily protect?
options: A database from every possible threat
blocks.explanation: TLS protects communication; application access controls remain necessary.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should you do if an API secret is exposed?
options: Post it to ask for help
Leave it active if the app still works
Revoke or rotate it and investigate where it was used
blocks.explanation: A leaked secret should be treated as compromised.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Copy all customer records for convenience
Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
